basedOn: Fi Zilal al-Quran, Sayyid Qutb (1906-1966), read from the Urdu rendering
blocks:
## What this verse does

The surah opens with "In the Name of Allah—the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful". Notice that it is not a statement about Allah so much as an act of beginning. The reader does not launch into praise on his own authority. He starts by naming the One he is about to address, the way a letter opens with the name of the person it is written to.

The two names carry the whole attitude of what follows. **Allah** is the name for the One who is worshipped, the name that belongs to Him alone and that no created thing shares. The other two are descriptions of how He treats what He has made.

**Most Compassionate** renders *ar-Rahman*. This is a word used only for Allah. A person cannot be called *rahman*, because it describes mercy that is vast by nature rather than earned by anything the receiver did.

**Most Merciful** renders *ar-Rahim*. This is the same root, in a form that can describe a person, and it points to mercy that actually arrives: the kindness shown, in this life and on the Day of Judgment. So the verse names one mercy that exists in Allah always and another that reaches His creatures in practice.

## Why it matters that the surah starts here

It would be possible to open a book about God with His power. This one opens with His mercy, before it says a word about mastery or judgment. That order is deliberate. The reader is told who is speaking before he is told what is demanded, so that everything hard in the surah that follows is heard as coming from a Merciful Lord and not a cold one.

This is also why the line is said at the head of every surah and at the start of every significant act: eating, travelling, writing, teaching.

## In short

- The verse is an act of beginning, not a description: the reader starts in Allah's name rather than his own.
- *Allah* is His proper name, shared with nothing created.
- "Most Compassionate" is mercy that belongs to Him by nature. "Most Merciful" is the same mercy arriving at His creatures.
- The surah starts with mercy before it mentions judgment, and that order sets the tone for all that follows.

## What this verse does

"All praise is for Allah—Lord of all worlds". The speaker has named Allah in verse 1 and now says something about Him. This is the first claim of the surah, and it is made as a statement of fact rather than a request.

The word translated "all praise" is *al-hamd*. It reaches wider than thanks. Thanking is for something done for you. *hamd* covers what a thing is as well as what it does. Praising a person's kindness is *hamd*. Praising their skill is *hamd* as well. The "all" matters, because it leaves no kind of praise outside Allah's right to it.

## The two halves of the sentence

**"All praise is for Allah"** says where praise belongs. Not to the sun, not to an idol, not to a ruler, not to the reader's own effort. Everything worth admiring in the world traces back to the One who made it, so the praise goes to Him.

**"Lord of all worlds"** says why. The word is *Rabb*, which means more than "owner". It carries the sense of someone who raises a thing stage by stage until it is complete: a parent raising a child, a gardener bringing a plant to fruit. Allah is *Rabb* of the *alamin*, which means every kind of created being there is, all of them together.

Put the two together and the logic is plain. If He is the one who brings everything into being and brings it along, then He is the one to whom everything's worth is owed.

## Why this belongs in a prayer

This verse is recited in every unit of prayer, which means a Muslim says it at least seventeen times a day. It is not decoration. It is the answer to a question the reader has not asked yet: why worship at all? Because everything the reader has came from Him, and praise is the only honest response to that.

Notice also who is speaking. In verse 1 the reader spoke about Allah. Here the reader is still speaking about Him, but the words are given, so that a person who cannot find the right words to praise God is handed a sentence that is already correct.

## In short

- The verse states a claim rather than making a request: all praise belongs to Allah.
- *Al-hamd* covers praise for what a thing is, not only thanks for what it does.
- *Rabb* means the one who raises and completes, so "Lord of all worlds" is about constant care, not distant ownership.
- Because He is the source of everything, praise is owed to Him and the reader is given the words to give it.

## What this verse does

"the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful". These are the same two names that appeared in verse 1, and here they are repeated as a verse of their own. Repetition in the Qur'an usually signals emphasis rather than forgetfulness, and this is the clearest case of it: the surah stops to say the same thing twice.

## Why say it again here

In verse 2 the reader has just called Allah "Lord of all worlds". That is a description of enormous distance. A lord of every world there is could sound like a power so far above a single person that the person's small life hardly registers. Verse 3 answers that fear before it forms. The Lord of all worlds is *ar-Rahman* and *ar-Rahim*, mercy by nature and mercy in practice. The same Being who runs everything is the one whose attention reaches the individual.

So the repetition is not padding. It is the point where the surah makes sure the reader has understood that grandeur and tenderness are not opposites here.

## What the two names add to each other

*Ar-Rahman* is mercy as an attribute of Allah: a quality that cannot be switched off and cannot be earned. It is a word the language reserves for Him.

*Ar-Rahim* is that attribute in action, arriving at creatures. It can describe a human being, because humans can show mercy, however imperfectly.

One is the ocean, the other is the water reaching your hands. Together they say that Allah's mercy is not just a fact about Him but something He does, continually, and to whoever is in front of Him.

## A contrast worth knowing

The surah is quietly drawing a line here. Older religious pictures often had gods who were brilliant and capricious, who had to be bribed and managed, whose favour was never secure. This verse asserts the opposite: the Lord of everything is merciful by nature before He asks anything of you. The reader comes into the surah already welcomed, and everything after this is heard from inside that welcome.

## In short

- These are the names from verse 1, repeated as a verse in their own right for emphasis.
- They are placed directly after "Lord of all worlds", to stop that grandeur from sounding distant.
- *Ar-Rahman* is mercy that belongs to Allah's nature and cannot be earned. *ar-Rahim* is that mercy reaching His creatures.
- The verse tells the reader he is addressed by mercy before he is asked for anything.

## What this verse does

"Master of the Day of Judgment". After three verses of praise, the surah names the fact that people usually prefer not to think about: there is a day when everything is settled and nothing is forgotten.

The word translated "Master" is *Malik*, which means owner and holder of authority over a thing. The surah uses it of a day, which is an unusual thing to own. The point is that the day belongs to Him, runs on His terms, and no one else sets its rulings.

## What "the Day of Judgment" means

The Arabic is *Yawm ad-Din*. *Din* here means recompense, the settling of accounts, not the religion a person follows. The phrase the app uses, "the Day of Judgment", is accurate: a day on which judgment is passed and each thing is paid what it is owed.

## Why this verse had to come when it did

The first three verses say Allah is merciful. A reader could hear only that and conclude that nothing he does will ever matter. This verse closes that gap: the same Lord is also the one who will call every deed to account. Mercy and accountability are said in the same breath, and the surah refuses to let either cancel the other.

It also answers something the reader already senses. Anyone who has seen injustice go unpunished has wanted a day like this. The verse says the desire is not naive. The day is real, and it is owned by the One who can pull it off.

## What it asks of the reader

Holding this verse in mind changes how the rest of the surah is read. A person who knows he will be judged does not approach Allah casually. He asks for guidance, which is what verses 5 to 7 do. The verse also quietly removes any idea that standing before Allah is about impressing other people, because on that day no one else's opinion counts.

## In short

- The surah turns from praise to accountability, naming the Day of Judgment as a fact rather than a threat.
- *Malik* means owner and authority: the day belongs to Allah and runs by His rule.
- *Din* here means the settling of accounts, which is why "Judgment" is the right translation.
- The verse is placed after the mercy verses so that mercy is not mistaken for indifference.

## What this verse does

"You ˹alone˺ we worship and You ˹alone˺ we ask for help". This is the hinge of the surah. Everything before it was about Allah. Everything after it is a request. Here, for the first time, the reader speaks directly to Him.

The verse is emphatic in a way the English has to stretch to show. In Arabic, the object is placed before the verb and again before the second verb, so the sense is "You, and no one else, we worship. You, and no one else, we ask for help". That doubled *alone* is the engine of the verse.

## The two halves

**"You alone we worship"** is a promise. It says the reader will direct his service to Allah and not divide it among others: not to idols, not to wealth, not to the approval of other people, not to his own ego dressed up as principle.

**"You alone we ask for help"** is an admission. Anyone can claim to worship Allah alone. It is harder to admit that help is needed at all, and harder still to ask only Him for it. This half says that reliance on Allah is total, so no created power is treated as the real source of rescue.

Note the order. Worship comes before asking. The surah does not open the relationship with demands. It begins with loyalty and then, from that position, admits a need.

## The plural, and what it does

The verse says "we", not "I". A solitary reader is folded into a community every time he recites it. Prayer is not a private transaction but a shared stance: the person next to you, and the whole body of believers across time, are saying the same sentence.

## Why this is the hinge

The surah has established that Allah is merciful, the Lord of everything, and the judge of the final day. A person who believes all of that has exactly one honest response, and this verse words it. The consequence of all that identity is total loyalty, and the rest of the surah flows out of it: if help comes from Him alone, then what the reader asks for next is the help he most needs.

## Freeing, not narrowing

It is worth noticing what exclusive worship removes. If no created thing deserves worship, then no ruler, employer, party, or family can claim the obedience that belongs to Allah. The verse is a declaration of independence from every false authority, and it is stated as a matter of worship rather than politics.

## In short

- The verse is the turning point: the reader stops talking about Allah and speaks to Him.
- Grammatically it says "You alone" twice, once for worship and once for help, which is why the translation adds ˹alone˺.
- Worship is placed before asking, so the relationship begins with loyalty rather than need.
- "We" binds the reader to every other believer who recites it. "Alone" frees him from every other claim on his obedience.

## What this verse does

"Guide us along the Straight Path". Having declared that help is sought from Allah alone, the reader now says what help he wants. Of all the things a person could ask for, this is the request the surah puts in his mouth.

## What is being asked for

The word translated "guide" is not only "show me where the road is". It also means keeping a person steady on the road once he is on it and bringing him through to the end. So the prayer asks for more than information a person lacks. It asks for the strength to keep going with what he already knows.

"The Straight Path" is one road, not a general direction. It means the way of life Allah set out as correct, the path the prophets walked, the route that arrives at Him safely. A person who already knows this path still prays for it every prayer, because knowing a road and travelling it are different things.

## Why guidance comes first

The surah has just said that help is asked of Allah alone. Now the first thing asked for is guidance. That order says something about what the reader thinks his greatest need is. Not longer life, not wealth, not the removal of hardship, but the ability to be on the right road. Everything else is counted as secondary to that.

## Who is really asking

The speaker is already guided, in the sense that he is praying. So the verse is not the cry of a stranger looking for the road. It is the prayer of a traveller asking to stay found. That is why it is repeated so often. The danger is not only never starting, but drifting off.

## In short

- This is the first thing the surah asks for after declaring that help comes from Allah alone.
- "Guide" carries the sense of keeping someone on the road to the end, not just pointing it out.
- "The Straight Path" is a specific way of life, not a vague direction.
- Even a person already walking it asks again every prayer, because staying on a road is a daily need.

## What this verse does

"the Path of those You have blessed—not those You are displeased with, or those who are astray". The surah ends by filling in what the Straight Path is and is not. Guidance, the previous verse asked for, is described here by example rather than definition.

## The three groups

**"those You have blessed"** are the people who received Allah's favour and walked his way rightly. The surah's answer to "which path?" is not an abstract rule but the route those people actually took, which makes it something a reader can follow rather than merely agree with.

**"those You are displeased with"** are people who knew the truth and turned away from it. The defining failure here is not ignorance. It is knowing and then refusing.

**"those who are astray"** are people who lost the road without having known it in the first place, or who wandered off without aiming to defy anything.

The two negative cases are different, and the verse keeps them separate on purpose. One group broke away knowingly. The other drifted, or never found it. Both are pitfalls, and asking to be kept from both is part of asking for the road.

## Why the verse is worded by example

A list of rules can be argued with and edited. A list of people is harder to escape, because it forces the reader to ask which group he is actually in. The surah closes by putting three crowds in front of him and inviting him to see which one he is walking behind.

## What it asks of the reader

The verse is a warning wrapped in a prayer. It is asking to be kept from becoming the sort of person whose failure is either refusal or wandering. And because it was just said that praise belongs to Allah alone and that help is asked from Him alone, the request is not fatalistic: the reader is asking to be steered, and the asking itself is the steering beginning.

## In short

- Guidance is defined by example: people who were favoured, people who turned away knowingly, people who wandered.
- "Those You are displeased with" are defined by knowing and refusing, not by ignorance.
- "Those who are astray" are defined by losing the road rather than rejecting it.
- The two failures are kept separate because both are dangers, and the verse asks to be held back from each.
